headline: Compare prefix pairs without requiring adjacency
statement: Return the length of the longest common subsequence of text1 and text2. A subsequence preserves relative character order but may skip characters. Return zero if no character sequence is common.
constraints: Both strings contain lowercase English letters
intuition: Compare prefixes of the two strings. If their final characters match, add one to the answer for the two shorter prefixes. Otherwise, keep the better answer from dropping either final character. Save these smaller answers in rows so the same prefix pair is not solved repeatedly.
approach: Start a zero row representing an empty text1 prefix.
For each text1 character, build a row over text2: match uses diagonal+1, mismatch uses max(above,left).
Replace the previous row and return its final value.
correctness: If the last characters match, a best possible common subsequence can include that match after a best possible shorter-prefix subsequence. If they differ, they cannot both end the same subsequence, so dropping either last character covers the best possible result. Induction over both prefix lengths proves the recurrence.
bruteForce: List all subsequences of one string and check each against the other; there are up to 2^m candidates.

complexity.explanation: Each prefix pair is computed once; only two length-n rows are retained.

pitfalls: Subsequence characters need not be adjacent.
Matching uses the previous diagonal, not the current row value.
A mismatch chooses a maximum; it does not reset the cell to zero as substring DP would.
